subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: fixing a total budget and working backward [Thinking]
passage: Before our Mysore trip last winter, everyone in the group chat was already choosing ice creams. I'm Pranav, and I was the one holding the notebook. Each of us had 3,000 rupees from the school trip kitty. Madhuri said, "Start from the top, not from the fun stuff." So I wrote 3,000 and began taking things away. Bus there and back: 1,150. Two nights in the dormitory: 1,050. I stared at what was left. 800. For two and a half days of meals, the palace ticket, the zoo and any water we'd buy. My stomach dropped a little, honestly. I read it out on our call and the chat went quiet. Then Madhuri said, "Good. Now we know the real number." We cut the zoo and kept the palace. Looking back, that one subtraction saved us from a very hungry last day.

qa.q: How much did the two nights in the dormitory cost each person?
qa.a: The two nights in the dormitory cost 1,050.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when the number 800 appeared, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Pranav felt a jolt of worry; the narrator says their stomach dropped a little on seeing how little was left for meals and tickets.

qa.q: What else could the group try if 800 still felt too tight?
qa.a: They could look for a cheaper stay or carry some snacks from home, then redo the subtraction together before booking, so every choice rests on the real number.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see the quiet moment in the chat?
qa.a: Madhuri treats it as useful rather than bad news, because knowing the real number early lets the group decide calmly what to cut.

grounding: Shows teens starting from each person's fixed trip money, subtracting bus and stay first, and finding only 800 left for meals and tickets.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: fixing a total budget and working backward [Thinking]
passage:
Class 9B trip planning, Thursday. Notes by the class teacher.
The group wanted to begin with the coracle ride at Hampi. I asked them to start from the other end instead. Parveen wrote 3,000 at the top of the board, the amount each student has. Vishal read out the train fare, 1,300 return, and Parveen took it away. Then the guesthouse, 900 for two nights. "So... 800 for everything else?" Vishal said, and laughed nervously. Parveen kept going, half under her breath: "Three days, six meals at least, the site tickets. The coracle is 300. That's too big a piece of 800." Nobody argued. They crossed out the ride and wrote "maybe, if money is left" beside it.
Next step: on Monday I will bring the guesthouse's menu prices so they can test the food part of the plan.

qa.q: What was the return train fare?
qa.a: The train fare was 1,300 return.

qa.q: How can you tell that Parveen was worried about the coracle ride?
qa.a: Parveen sounded concerned, listing the meals and site tickets still to be paid and saying 300 was too big a piece of the 800.

qa.q: What would you change first if the guesthouse menu turns out costly?
qa.a: The group could plan some meals at cheaper local stalls, then redo the subtraction with the new food cost before adding back any extra ride.

qa.q: How might Vishal see the plan once the ride was crossed out?
qa.a: Vishal may be a little let down about the ride but also relieved to know the real limit, since Vishal's nervous laugh showed the 800 was a surprise.

grounding: Illustrates a group working backward from each student's fixed trip amount, taking away train fare and stay to see that only 800 remains for food and tickets.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: comparing transport and stay options [Thinking]
passage: So you asked how we got to Goa without blowing our money. Okay, I'm Joseph, and the spreadsheet was Devika's idea, but I did the arguing part. We had three choices for the overnight leg from Pune. The shared taxi was fastest, maybe nine hours, but even split four ways it cost the most, and we didn't know the driver or who else would squeeze in. The bus was cheap, but it reached a highway stop at three in the morning. The sleeper train took almost twelve hours. I kept saying, "Twelve hours is so long, yaar." Then Devika asked me, "Long compared to what? We'll be asleep." That flipped it for me. Cheaper than the taxi, a safer arrival time than the bus, and the extra hours cost us nothing while we sleep. We booked the train that night.

qa.q: How long did the sleeper train take?
qa.a: The sleeper train took almost twelve hours.

qa.q: Why was Joseph unhappy with the train at first?
qa.a: Joseph felt impatient about losing so much time, complaining that twelve hours was so long, until Devika pointed out they would be asleep.

qa.q: What else could the group compare before booking?
qa.a: They could check how they would get from the station to their stay after the train arrives, so the cheaper, safer choice stays safe at the other end too.

qa.q: How does Devika see the hours the train takes?
qa.a: Devika sees the long journey as costing them little, since they sleep through it, so the lower price and safer arrival matter more to Devika.

grounding: Shows students weighing a shared taxi, a bus and a sleeper train on price, time and safety, and accepting the slower overnight train to save money.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: comparing transport and stay options [Thinking]
passage: I was only half-watching TV when my cousin Siddharth and his classmate Afreen spread three printouts across the dining table. Their class was going from Ahmedabad to Udaipur and they had to pick the night journey. Afreen read the numbers out: shared taxi 1,200 each, overnight bus 650, sleeper train 520. "Taxi's out," Siddharth said quickly. Afreen tapped the bus sheet. "Cheap, but look, it's a small operator with no reviews, and it drops us on the bypass at four." Siddharth frowned at the train timing. "It's two hours slower though." They went quiet for a bit. Then Afreen said, "Slower is fine if we're lying down in a coach full of families." Siddharth nodded and circled the train. I couldn't tell whether he was fully convinced, but he didn't argue again.

qa.q: How much did the shared taxi cost each person?
qa.a: The shared taxi cost 1,200 each.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have been worried about when he frowned at the train timing?
qa.a: Siddharth seemed uneasy that the train was two hours slower, and even after circling it the cousin could not tell if he felt fully convinced.

qa.q: Which other check would suit the pair before they book?
qa.a: They could ask the class teacher or their parents to look over the choice and confirm who meets them at the station, since safety was part of why they chose the train.

qa.q: How does the cousin see the way Afreen and Siddharth decided?
qa.a: The cousin watches them sort the options quickly and sensibly, but admits only guessing at what Siddharth really felt, beyond the fact that he stopped arguing.

grounding: Shows two students comparing a shared taxi, a bus and a sleeper train on price, time and safety, and picking the slower train for the night leg.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: dividing planning tasks among the group [Action]
passage: Ines drew four boxes on the back of a café napkin. "Transport, food, beds, safety. One each." Yosef took transport, Marta took food, Duarte took the hostel, and Ines kept safety: emergency numbers, a meeting point, and what their parents needed to know. "Everything goes in the shared sheet," she said. "Prices, links, one line each. Deadline is Friday at eight. Whatever's in by then, we decide on." By Wednesday Yosef had train and coach prices for the Lisbon to Porto run. Duarte found two hostels and a small guesthouse. Marta added a supermarket picnic plan next to a café option. On Friday evening they sat on Ines's bedroom floor, scrolled the sheet once, and chose everything in twenty minutes. For once, nobody had spent three nights searching the same things twice.

qa.q: Which job did Duarte take?
qa.a: Duarte took the hostel.

qa.q: Why did Ines set a Friday deadline?
qa.a: Ines seemed determined to keep the planning calm and fair, wanting a fixed point so nobody would feel stuck searching everything twice.

qa.q: What else could help if one friend missed the Friday deadline?
qa.a: The group could agree ahead of time that a missing part gets the simplest safe option, or have a quick call with that friend, so one gap does not stall everyone.

qa.q: How might Yosef see having only transport to research?
qa.a: Yosef can go deep on train and coach prices without chasing the rest, which likely feels lighter than planning the whole trip alone.

grounding: Shows four friends splitting transport, food, stay and safety, pooling quotes in one shared sheet and deciding by an agreed deadline.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: dividing planning tasks among the group [Action]
passage: By Tuesday, Jaya and Raghav had each spent an evening comparing the same three bus companies. They found out only in the hostel common room, when they held up identical screenshots. "That's two hours each, gone," Raghav groaned. Kabir and Meera looked up from the carrom board. Jaya pulled a chart paper off the notice board. "Okay. Four jobs, four people." Raghav kept transport, since he'd already started. Jaya took the stay near Rishikesh, Meera took food, and Kabir took safety: the warden's permission slips, a first-aid kit, emergency contacts. They made one shared sheet with a tab for each job and pinned the link in the hostel group. "All quotes by Sunday night," Jaya said. "Monday after assembly, we choose." The warden, passing by, read the chart and initialled the corner.

qa.q: What did Jaya pull off the notice board?
qa.a: Jaya pulled a chart paper off the notice board.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when he saw the identical screenshots?
qa.a: Raghav felt frustrated about the wasted effort, groaning that two hours each were gone.

qa.q: What would you change first if the Sunday deadline slipped?
qa.a: They could still meet on Monday and decide with whatever quotes are in, filling any gap with the simplest safe choice rather than delaying everything.

qa.q: How might Kabir see the job of handling safety?
qa.a: Kabir may feel trusted with an important part, and keeping slips, first aid and contacts in one place means the others need not worry about them.

grounding: Illustrates friends dividing transport, stay, food and safety, sharing quotes in one sheet and setting a deadline after they duplicated work.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: involving parents and choosing safe arrangements [Action]
passage:
Subject: Coorg trip plan (please read, Amma and Appa!)

Hi Amma, Appa,
You asked for everything in writing, so here it is.
Dates: 14 to 16 October. We leave Mysuru on the 7 am bus.
Stay: Greenhill Youth Hostel, Madikeri. The address and phone number are attached. I checked, and it has separate dorms for girls and boys.
Adult with us: Chaitanya's aunt, Revathi Aunty. She is coming for all three days, and her number is in the attachment too.
Check-ins: I'll call you at 9 pm every night, and message when we reach and leave each place.
If plans change, I'll tell you before we change them, not after.
I know you're nervous about me going without you. I would feel better too, knowing you have every detail. Can we talk about it at dinner tonight?
Love,
Sudha

qa.q: What time will the nightly check-in call be?
qa.a: The call will be at 9 pm every night.

qa.q: What does Sudha think the parents are feeling about the trip?
qa.a: Sudha senses they are nervous about the trip without them, and hopes the full details will reassure them.

qa.q: What else could make the plan even safer?
qa.a: All the parents could get one shared contact list, and the group could agree a meeting point in Madikeri in case anyone gets separated.

qa.q: How might Revathi Aunty see her role on the trip?
qa.a: As the responsible adult for all three days, she may appreciate that the teens shared times and contacts, since it makes looking after them easier.

grounding: Shows a teen giving parents the dates, hostel details, contact numbers and nightly check-in times, and travelling with a responsible adult.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: involving parents and choosing safe arrangements [Action]
passage: You know why Afreen's parents finally said yes to Shimla? Sit, I'll tell you. I'm Rukmini, the one who nagged everyone into making a folder. The first time we asked, her Abbu said no in one second. Fair enough, we had only said, "Shimla, three days, please." So we made a real plan. A printed itinerary with every stop and timing. The hostel's name, address and landline. All four of our numbers, plus our geography teacher's, because Mr. Thapa agreed to come with us. Then we sat with all the parents one Sunday and asked them to choose the check-in times. They picked a morning call and a night call. Afreen's Abbu read every page, asked about the hill road after dark, and then signed. That folder did more than any amount of begging.

qa.q: Who agreed to come with the group?
qa.a: Their geography teacher, Mr. Thapa, agreed to come with them.

qa.q: Why wasn't Rukmini upset by the first no?
qa.a: Rukmini felt it was fair, since they had asked so vaguely, and was determined to answer the parents' worries with a real plan instead of begging.

qa.q: What else could the group do if a parent still felt unsure?
qa.a: They could invite that parent to call Mr. Thapa or the hostel directly, so the adult checks the arrangements personally.

qa.q: How might Afreen's Abbu see the plan at the Sunday meeting?
qa.a: He can see where his daughter will be and who is responsible, and choosing the check-in times gives him a say, which likely eases his worry about the night road.

grounding: Illustrates teens sharing an itinerary, hostel details and contact numbers with parents, agreeing check-in times and travelling with a teacher, so the trip is approved.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: buffer for delays and extra costs [Thinking]
passage: Yash's plan for the Darjeeling trip looked almost boring. Tenzin, reading it over his shoulder at the station, pointed at one line: "Spare: 450 (10% of 4,500)." "Why keep money doing nothing?" "Because something always goes wrong," Yash said. "And every day has one empty hour. See, after lunch." Tenzin shrugged. Then the announcement came: their train from Siliguri was running ninety minutes late. Rain had slowed everything on the line. Tenzin groaned. Yash was already recounting. "We lose today's empty hour, plus a bit. So we skip the tea shop and still reach the homestay before dark." In Darjeeling, the shared jeep to the monastery cost more than the website had said. Yash paid the difference from the spare. By day three, the plan had bent twice and nothing had broken.

qa.q: How late was the train from Siliguri?
qa.a: The train from Siliguri was running ninety minutes late.

qa.q: What does Yash's quick recounting suggest about how he felt when the delay was announced?
qa.a: Yash stayed calm rather than panicked, because the spare hour meant a delay was a problem he had already expected.

qa.q: What else could Yash try if a delay ran much longer than the spare hour?
qa.a: He could decide in advance which stop is first to drop each day, so a big delay means one quick cut instead of a scramble.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see the boring spare line by day three?
qa.a: Tenzin, who shrugged it off at first, likely sees its worth after the delay and the costlier jeep, since the empty hour and the spare money kept the trip on track.

grounding: Shows a teen keeping a ten percent money reserve and a spare hour each day, so a late train and a higher jeep fare do not wreck the plan.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: buffer for delays and extra costs [Thinking]
passage: "Just fill every hour, na," Tushar said, scrolling the list of Mumbai sights on Ramesh's laptop in the colony reading room. Ramesh shook his head. "Last year our class missed the aquarium because the bus got stuck in traffic for an hour. Everything after that fell like dominoes." He typed a line into each day: "Free hour, 3 to 4." Then under money: "2,000 each, keep 200 aside." "Ten percent for what?" "Prices change. Or someone's slipper breaks. If we don't need it, we eat something nice on the last night." On Saturday, the ferry to Elephanta cost forty rupees more each than the price they had found online. Tushar paid it from the kept-aside money without a word, then grinned at Ramesh. "Fine. Your boring hour can stay too."

qa.q: How much did Ramesh plan to keep aside out of 2,000 each?
qa.a: Ramesh planned to keep 200 aside.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh insist on a free hour each day?
qa.a: Ramesh was still wary after last year, when one hour stuck in traffic made everything after it fall like dominoes.

qa.q: What else could help if a delay and a price rise hit on the same day?
qa.a: They could choose in advance one sight to drop first, so the free hour and the spare money cover the rest without an argument on the spot.

qa.q: How does Tushar see the buffer by Saturday?
qa.a: Tushar first wanted every hour filled, but after the ferry cost more, Tushar grins and accepts both the spare money and the free hour.

grounding: Illustrates a teen reasoning aloud for a ten percent reserve and a spare hour daily, which later absorbs a rise in the ferry price.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: overpacking the itinerary [Pitfall]
passage: Rafiq had written the list on the back of a wedding card: eight places in and around Chittorgarh, two days. Zainab had even bought the combined monument pass at the tourist office on Friday, eight stamps' worth, 250 rupees each. On Saturday the first local bus from their kasba left an hour late. Then the auto took the long road up to the fort because of a fair near the gate. By noon they had seen two places and were sitting on a step, sharing warm water. "The map made it look like ten minutes between each," Rafiq muttered. On Sunday Zainab's feet were blistered. They saw two more, skipped the rest, and caught the evening bus home. Zainab held up her pass, four boxes still blank. "Two hundred and fifty rupees each for half a trip."

qa.q: Where had Rafiq written the list of places?
qa.a: Rafiq had written the list on the back of a wedding card.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling while muttering about the map?
qa.a: Rafiq felt tired and frustrated, seeing that the ten minutes the map suggested between places had been far too hopeful.

qa.q: What would you change first when planning the next two-day trip?
qa.a: They could pick three or four places, check real travel times by bus and auto, and buy passes only for places they are sure to reach.

qa.q: How is Zainab affected by the packed plan?
qa.a: Zainab ends up with blistered feet and a half-used pass she paid for in advance, so the plan costs her both comfort and money.

grounding: Shows teens cramming eight places into two days, getting worn out by slow buses and autos, skipping half and wasting the pass they bought.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: overpacking the itinerary [Pitfall]
passage: Beatriz's spreadsheet for their school's two-day London trip had eight rows and neat colour codes. Soo-ah had asked about walking times, but Beatriz waved it off: "It's all close on the map." They pre-booked timed tickets for the tower at two o'clock and a river cruise at five. By eleven on day one, they were still stuck in the bag queue at the second museum. The underground was packed, and one line was suspended. They reached the tower at quarter to three, and the gate staff said their slot had passed. The cruise went the same way. On day two, Soo-ah sat on a bench outside the fourth place and refused to walk another step. "We saw four," she said quietly, rubbing her heels. "And we paid for two we never saw."

qa.q: What time was the tower slot?
qa.a: The tower tickets were for two o'clock.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling when she refused to walk another step?
qa.a: Soo-ah was exhausted and quietly frustrated, since her question about walking times had been waved off and now they had paid for tickets they never used.

qa.q: Which approach would suit this group better next time?
qa.a: Planning fewer places a day with honest travel and queue times, and booking timed tickets only after that, would leave room for delays.

qa.q: How might Beatriz see the spreadsheet after day two?
qa.a: Beatriz may feel embarrassed that the colour-coded plan ignored how slow queues and trains can be, and sorry that Soo-ah's early question was brushed aside.

grounding: Illustrates an overpacked two-day plan that ignores travel and queue time, so half the places are skipped and paid tickets go unused.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: ignoring hidden costs [Pitfall]
passage: Rajni's budget for the three-day Kolkata trip fit on one sticky note: train 700, guesthouse share 900, museum tickets 300. Total 1,900, and she had 2,200. "Three hundred spare, easy," she told Nazia on the platform. Nobody had written down the autos from Howrah, the bottles of water in the heat, the jhalmuri at every corner, or the extra fee to take a camera into one museum. On the third morning, Rajni opened her wallet outside the guesthouse and found forty rupees. The last stop was the science centre, with its own entry fee, and then a cab back to the station. Her face went hot. Nazia didn't ask anything; she just held out two hundred. "Pay me back at school." Rajni took it, staring at the sticky note.

qa.q: How much money did Rajni have for the trip?
qa.a: Rajni had 2,200.

qa.q: What does Rajni's hot face suggest?
qa.a: Rajni felt embarrassed at running short and needing a friend's money after being so sure of the three hundred spare.

qa.q: What else could Rajni have done while planning?
qa.a: Rajni could have listed the small daily costs like autos, water, snacks and entry fees, or asked someone who had made the trip what they really spent.

qa.q: How might Nazia see lending the two hundred?
qa.a: Nazia seems glad to help without questions, though her own money shrinks and she has to wait to be paid back at school.

grounding: Shows a student budgeting only for train, stay and main tickets, forgetting autos, water, snacks and fees, and borrowing from a friend on the last day.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: ignoring hidden costs [Pitfall]
passage:
"Salma, how much do you have left?"
"About six hundred. Why?"
"I have ninety. Ninety, Salma."
"What? Nikita, you had the whole thing planned. Bus, hostel, the cable car."
"I know! I planned for those. I didn't plan for the shared jeeps every morning. Or water, it's thirty a bottle up here."
"And the momos."
"And the momos. And that entry fee at the waterfall nobody told us about."
"Okay. What's left today?"
"Jeep to the bus stand, lunch, and the ticket at the lookout. Maybe two hundred."
"Take two fifty. Just in case."
"I'll pay you back the day we're home. I'm so sorry."
"Stop. Next trip, you plan the small stuff with me, deal?"
"Deal. A whole column just for water."
"And one for momos."

qa.q: How much money does Nikita have left?
qa.a: Nikita has ninety left.

qa.q: How does Nikita feel when asking Salma for money?
qa.a: Nikita feels ashamed and anxious about borrowing, apologising after having planned the big costs so carefully.

qa.q: What would you change first in the budget for the next trip?
qa.a: A column for daily small costs like jeeps, water, snacks and surprise entry fees would show the real total before leaving.

qa.q: How might Salma see lending the money?
qa.a: Salma treats it calmly and kindly and wants to plan the small costs together next time, though lending two fifty leaves Salma with less for the day as well.

grounding: Illustrates a student who planned bus, hostel and cable car but forgot jeeps, water, snacks and fees, and borrows from a friend on the last day.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: going along with the loudest friend [Pitfall]
passage:
Youth group log, Sunday evening. Written by the group leader.
During trip planning today, Thomas suggested the adventure park near Lonavala: zip line, rope course, the works. Entry is 1,800 per head. He was so excited that the group clapped and moved straight on to choosing a date. Nobody mentioned cost. I noticed Maria stopped writing in her notebook and looked at the floor. Later, while stacking chairs, she asked me quietly whether the trip was "compulsory". Joel, who usually talks the most, left early without saying goodbye. I don't know their situations and I won't guess, but two quiet faces right after a big price is something I should not ignore.
Next steps: at Wednesday's meeting I'll ask everyone to write a comfortable spending limit on an unsigned slip before we choose. I'll also bring two cheaper options, so Thomas's idea isn't the only one on the table.

qa.q: How much is entry at the adventure park?
qa.a: Entry is 1,800 per head.

qa.q: What might Maria have been worried about when she asked if the trip was compulsory?
qa.a: Maria may have been anxious about affording the 1,800 entry and felt unable to say so in front of the excited group.

qa.q: Which approach would suit the group better when choosing a trip?
qa.a: Agreeing a cost range before hearing ideas, for example with unsigned slips, lets quieter members be heard without explaining money worries in public.

qa.q: How might Thomas see the plan being reopened on Wednesday?
qa.a: Thomas may feel disappointed that his idea isn't settled, but seeing other options could help him notice that not everyone could afford it.

grounding: Shows a group accepting one boy's costly adventure park idea without talking about money, while two members go quiet and struggle to object.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: going along with the loudest friend [Pitfall]
passage:
Tuesday, late
Ojas has decided our Class 10 farewell trip is the water park. 1,500 each plus the bus. He announced it in the group chat with twelve exclamation marks, and everyone sent a thumbs up within two minutes. I sent one too. Why did I do that?
Papa's shop has been slow since the rains. I already asked for the exam form fee last month. I can't ask for 1,500 for water slides.
In the canteen Ritika whispered, "Is it very costly or is it just me?" So it's not just me. But she didn't say anything in the group either.
Ojas keeps saying, "Best day of our lives, guys!" If I say it's too much now, I'll be the one who ruined it.
Maybe I just won't go. I hate that this is the only plan I have.
Uday

qa.q: How much does the water park cost each?
qa.a: It costs 1,500 each plus the bus.

qa.q: Why did Uday send a thumbs up despite the cost?
qa.a: Uday felt pressured by how fast everyone agreed and was afraid of being the one who ruined the plan, so the worry stayed hidden.

qa.q: What else could Uday try instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Uday and Ritika could ask together, in the group or privately to Ojas, for a cheaper option, which is easier than one person objecting alone.

qa.q: How is Ritika affected by the way the plan was decided?
qa.a: Ritika also finds it too costly but feels unable to speak up in the group, so she carries the same quiet worry and only whispers it.

grounding: Illustrates a group going along with one boy's costly plan without discussing money, while two members privately struggle to afford it.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: replanning when a booking fails [Revision]
passage:
"Madhav, the hostel just replied. They're full. Our booking never went through."
"What? We leave on Friday, Asif!"
"Okay, okay. Breathe. We had two backups on the list. The guesthouse near the lake and the youth hostel by the bus stand."
"You call the guesthouse, I'll call the youth hostel."
"Youth hostel has beds. Four hundred a night, fifty more than ours was."
"Guesthouse has a room, but it's six hundred."
"Amma! Can you come here a minute?"
"What happened?"
"Our hostel's full. This one's by the bus stand. Here's the page, and here's their number. Can you call them once?"
"Give it to me... Fine. They sound proper, and it's close to the stop. You can book it."
"So a hundred more each for the two nights. Take it from food?"
"Fifty less a day on snacks. I'll change the sheet now and tell the group."

qa.q: How much does the youth hostel cost a night?
qa.a: The youth hostel costs four hundred a night.

qa.q: How does Madhav feel on hearing the booking failed?
qa.a: Madhav panics at first, worried because they leave on Friday, until Asif helps calm things down.

qa.q: What else could the group have done to avoid the last-minute scramble?
qa.a: They could have confirmed the booking by phone a week earlier while keeping the backups ready, so a full hostel would be a small change rather than a shock.

qa.q: How does the change look to Amma?
qa.a: Amma gets to check the new place herself by phone, so she can feel it is proper and close to the bus stop before agreeing.

grounding: Shows teens calling two backups when their hostel is full, getting a parent's approval, taking the extra cost from snacks and updating the shared plan.

subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: replanning when a booking fails [Revision]
passage: I still remember standing outside the hostel gate in Nainital with our bags, reading a paper sign: "Full. Sorry." Our online booking had simply vanished. I'm Kamal, and for about a minute I wanted to sit down on the road and cry. Usha didn't. She pulled out our list of backup places, handed me one number and dialled the other. Mine was a dharamshala near the market, 300 a night. Hers was a homestay, 550. We put Usha's father on speaker and read him both addresses, and he asked to talk to the homestay owner himself. Ten minutes later he called back: "The homestay. The family sounds careful." That was 250 more each for our one night, so we cut it from our food money and ate street noodles instead of café meals. I updated the shared sheet sitting on a bench.

qa.q: How much did the dharamshala cost a night?
qa.a: The dharamshala near the market cost 300 a night.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling on reading the sign?

passage: On the first night at the dharamshala in Vijayapura, Hafsa sat cross-legged under the tube light with a pencil and a small notebook. Tejas, on the next mat, asked what she was counting. "Today. Tonga 40, water 30, entry 25, lunch 220, peanuts 20." She frowned. "Three hundred thirty-five. We have 1,200 for three days, and that lunch is most of it." Hafsa asked the dharamshala caretaker, who pointed them to a khanavali behind the bus stand: jowar rotis, two sabzis, buttermilk, 70 a plate. The next night her page said 185. On the last night she added all three days, 810, and closed the notebook with a small, satisfied tap.
